title: Humans: A Monstrous History
description:
Surekha Davies's Humans: A Monstrous History reads the history of monster-making as a history of who gets to count as normal.

Davies traces how people have defined the human in relation to everything from apes to zombies, and how race, gender and nations were invented along the way. Her examples run from ancient gods and Frankenstein's monster to E.T. and generative AI. Her argument is that monster-making is about control. The University of California Press published it in February 2025 as a 336-page hardcover with ten color plates and forty black-and-white figures.

Davies is a British historian of science, art and ideas. Her first book, Renaissance Ethnography and the Invention of the Human, won the Morris D. Forkosch Prize and the Roland H. Bainton Prize. She has written essays and reviews for the Times Literary Supplement, Nature, Science and Aeon.

title: Harold's End
description:
JT LeRoy's Harold's End is a short, illustrated novella about a San Francisco street hustler, an older man, and a snail.

The narrator is Oliver, a youth on Polk Street feeding a heroin habit, who is taken in by a man named Larry. Larry provides shelter and drugs and takes an interest in Oliver's pet snail, Harold. The Last Gasp edition runs to 99 pages and is illustrated with eight watercolor paintings by the Australian artist Cherry Hood, each based on the story's character descriptions. Dave Eggers contributes an introduction. Last Gasp also issued signed copies, signed by LeRoy and Hood.

LeRoy's earlier books, Sarah and The Heart Is Deceitful Above All Things, were both international bestsellers, according to Last Gasp. Hood's watercolor of a boy holding a snail in a cup appears in miniature on the black cloth cover.

title: Zero: The Biography of a Dangerous Idea
description:
Charles Seife's Zero is a popular history of one number and the arguments it has set off in mathematics, philosophy, religion and physics.

Seife follows zero from its birth as an Eastern philosophical concept to its struggle for acceptance in Europe and its rise in the West. Along the way he covers the thinkers who tried to understand it, from Pythagoras and Newton to Heisenberg, and the clashes that pitted East against West and faith against reason. The book closes on zero in black holes, the Big Bang and the search for a theory of everything. This Penguin paperback is 256 pages.

Seife is a science journalist and a professor of journalism at New York University. Zero won the PEN/Martha Albrand Award for first nonfiction and was a New York Times Notable Book. His later books include Proofiness. He has written for the New York Times, Wired, New Scientist, Science, Scientific American and The Economist.
